title: One community services officer enforces city by-laws throughout 2016–2020
summary: Every financial plan presentation from 2016 to 2020 listed a single community services officer within protective services, alongside 16 RCMP officers and about 40 firefighters. In 2017 the presentation described the officer as the person 'who enforces city bylaws'. Council made no change to by-law enforcement staffing in this period.
status_detail: Staffing stayed at one officer across both terms; no motion or request to add officers was found. Weed, parking, animal and other by-law work fell to the same officer (2020 resident referred to him as 'the bylaws officer').
figures: Protective services budget: ~$3.1M (2016), ~$3.8M (2017), ~$4.1M (2018), $4.2M (2019), $4.2M (2020) (financial plan presentations, transcripts); 1 community services officer each year.
notes: Presenter identity for 2017 is medium confidence. Counts are from the 2016-02-16, 2017-02-21, 2018-03-20, 2019-03-19 and 2020-04-07 financial plan presentations.

title: Community services officer appointed weed inspector each year (routine)
summary: As required by The Noxious Weeds Act, council each year appointed the city's community services officer, Trevor Schellenberg, as municipal weed inspector. The items passed without debate beyond questions about the provincial cosmetic-pesticide ban (2016) and training (2016).
status_detail: Appointed for 2016 (transcript), 2018 (R18-052), 2019 (R19-121) and 2020 (R20-038), all unanimous. No 2017 appointment was found (the Apr 4, 2017 video is missing and no 2017 minutes before July exist). No enforcement figures were reported with any appointment.
decision_source: minutes (2018–2020); transcript (2016: moved by a Councillor Penner, seconded by Councillor Fehr)
notes: 2016 mover was 'Councillor Penner' (Cari or Susan, not determined).

title: Province's Community Safety Officer program letter sent to the RCMP advisory group
summary: Council received a Manitoba Justice letter on the new Community Safety Officer program. Councillor Funk asked what such officers would cost compared with the province-funded community constables; the City Manager said CSOs have limited powers and he was unsure Steinbach's conditions matched Thompson's pilot. The letter was taken as information and sent to the RCMP advisory group.
status_detail: No report back or decision on community safety officers was found in transcripts through Dec 2020.
reasons: cost: Asked what CSOs would cost the city when community constables were province-funded. (Earl Funk); study-first: Took the letter as information pending advice from the advisory group. (Chris Goertzen)
notes: The program concerned policing support more than property standards; included because later councils used community safety officers for by-law work.

title: Administrative Penalty By-law 2076 adopted, covering parking and traffic fines only
summary: Because the province's Municipal By-law Enforcement Act moved parking tickets out of provincial court, council adopted By-law 2076 (first reading Apr 11, 2017; second June 20; third July 4) to handle penalty notices with a municipal adjudicator. It applied at first to the traffic and accessible parking by-laws; By-law 2091 (Jan–Feb 2018) added the parking meter by-law. No property-standards, junk or weed by-law was added to the penalty schedule in this period.
status_detail: Adopted July 4, 2017 (transcript); amended by By-law 2091 (R18-010, R18-011 Jan 16, 2018; R18-024 Feb 6, 2018; unanimous). The penalty system was not extended to yard or property upkeep by Dec 2020.
figures: Accessible parking fine raised from $50 to $100 at the same time (By-law 2083; transcript 1:00:50, June 20, 2017); about $20,000 unbudgeted 2017 impact was for a different item.
reasons: enforcement-limits: Change was required by the province's Municipal By-law Enforcement Act (medium-confidence attribution). (Michael Zwaagstra)
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (2091 first and third readings); Susan Penner (2091 second)
notes: First reading (Apr 11, 2017) has no transcript. The 2017 second-reading mover 'Councillor Pinner' (label B) is probably Cari Penner (label B gave the opening introduced as 'Councillor Kerri Penner'); medium. Zwaagstra's 'no choice' remark (0:59:47, label E) is medium confidence and not quoted.

title: Resident asks who enforces weed by-laws on a vacant Main Street lot; no answer given
summary: At the July 17, 2018 hearing on the new zoning by-law and community plan, M.G. pointed to weeds on a vacant property on Main Street and an unsigned car lot, and asked whether anyone was enforcing the by-laws. Staff answered other questions; the enforcement question was not addressed.
status_detail: No response on the record at the hearing or later in 2018.
public: M.G. (Fernwood Bay) asked whether by-laws were being amended while 'nobody's carrying them out'.

title: Maplewood St rezoning (By-law 2101) denied 5–1 after neighbours say the owner let his rental houses run down
summary: An owner of a row of old rental houses at 135–191 Maplewood St asked to rezone them for 44 townhouses; his representative called most of the houses derelict. Neighbours (49 objection letters, 80-plus signatures) said he had owned some for up to 10 years without maintaining them and had not earned their trust. Council denied second reading 5–1; members cited unclear plans, drainage and lack of trust, while Councillor Susan Penner argued the new complex would be professionally maintained.
status_detail: Second reading denied (R18-191), so the by-law died. Council did not use any property-standards tool on the existing houses; Councillor Fehr said the properties 'really need to have some attention'.
figures: 44 units in 4 blocks of 11 (transcript 0:09:30); 49 notices of objection, over 84 signatures (transcript 0:28:33).
reasons: private-property: Lack of trust in the owner's upkeep record; the owner must regain the neighbourhood's trust before going forward. (Earl Funk)
public: D.M. (Albert St) presented objections that the owner had not made sufficient efforts to maintain the existing homes and had not earned residents' trust. Another Maplewood neighbour said the owner had refused to maintain the houses; another called them slums. These are residents' claims, unproven. The owner agreed the houses were old and 'not worth fixing up'.
notes: The owner and his representative are private individuals and are not named. 'Councillor Funk' here is Councillor Earl Funk (before he became mayor).

title: Residents say neighbours leave garbage outside for months; mayor rules it off topic
summary: At the Dec 4, 2018 hearing on renewing the garbage collection levy, two residents objected to the flat fee and also complained of litter and of neighbours leaving household garbage outside for months, drawing animals. The mayor said they were off topic; council renewed the levy unanimously without addressing the upkeep complaint.
status_detail: Levy by-law given second reading; the garbage-left-outside complaint got no response or referral.
public: M.G. said people throw garbage on lawns; A.O. said neighbours leave garbage outside for months and it attracts animals.
notes: Resolution number for the levy by-law second reading not checked.

title: Neighbours' complaints about a run-down rental at 126 Maplewood; council approves a 9-unit replacement
summary: At the hearing on By-law 2120 to rezone 126 Maplewood St for a 9-unit building, a 56-name petition opposed it. Neighbours said the landlords were slow with repairs and that the existing rental's backyard was 'an absolute disaster'. The owner said urgent repairs are done within two days. Council approved second reading unanimously, saying a new building would replace an old, run-down one.
status_detail: Neighbours' request to refuse was declined: second reading carried unanimously (R19-118, Zwaagstra/Siemens). The yard and repair complaints were answered with redevelopment, not enforcement.
reasons: already-doing-enough: Redevelopment will replace an older, run-down property with a new one. (Earl Funk); already-doing-enough: Replacing a facility 'which really shouldn't be there now' with a new one is an improvement. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: R.W. (Maplewood St) presented the petition and said the landlords were slow to fix a rental. W.C., the next-door neighbour, said the backyard and the bachelor suite were in terrible condition. These claims are unproven. Another speaker supported small units and said the fire commissioner had warned that many places in Steinbach were unsafe to live in (speaker's identity unclear in the transcript).
notes: Owners are private individuals and are not named (initials only for the applicant). Variance V-2019-11 was to follow third reading.

title: Councillor asks about the state of a rental at an 8-plex hearing; owner says upkeep is the tenant's job
summary: At a hearing for an 8-unit building on a C-1 lot at Elm Ave and Hanover St, Councillor Zwaagstra raised objectors' concerns about the current state of the property. The owner, who had owned it about two years, said his tenant knew they had to keep it up. Council denied the conditional use and variance unanimously for lack of consultation and neighbourhood character, not upkeep.
status_detail: Application denied (R19-140, R19-141, unanimous). The upkeep question got no follow-up; a Councillor Hiebert said the 'older place' was 'not well maintained'.
public: Neighbours (54-name petition) objected mainly to density, trees and lack of consultation; one said residents had been upgrading their homes.
notes: Minutes list the variance denial as Zwaagstra/J. Hiebert; the transcript chair names 'Councilor Pinner, seconded by Councilor Swaigstra'. The comment 'not well maintained' (0:55:27) is diarized under a label shared with other speakers, so it is not quoted.

title: Dwelling Units Safety Standards By-law 2157 given first reading (smoke alarms, CO alarms, escape exits)
summary: After a May 12, 2020 Strategic Priorities Committee report that a growing number of homes, mainly rental units, did not meet the Manitoba Building and Fire Codes or the zoning by-law, council directed staff to draft a by-law. On Sept 1, 2020 council unanimously gave By-law 2157 first reading. Members said it was 15 to 20 years in the making, limited to basic life-safety items (smoke alarms, carbon monoxide alarms, egress), and that the city did not know where all secondary suites were.
status_detail: First reading Sept 1, 2020 (R20-167). Second and third readings were given Jan 5, 2021 (R21-007, Zwaagstra/Siemens; R21-008, Siemens/J. Hiebert; both unanimous), just after this period. No public input on the by-law was found in the Sept–Dec 2020 transcripts or minutes; the Sept 15, 2020 meeting video is not available.
figures: Vacancy rate 'below 4%' (Siemens, transcript 0:21:02). Mayor Funk expected full compliance to take 'maybe a decade or two' (transcript 0:25:00). The May 12, 2020 SPC report was not available to us.
reasons: affordability: Warned renters of substandard units would likely pay more because upgrades could be substantial. (Jac Siemens); enforcement-limits: Said compliance won't happen overnight; a long project over 'maybe a decade or two'. (Earl Funk); study-first: First reading is the first step; the next is to hear the public before deciding how to move forward. (Jac Siemens)
public: No residents spoke to the by-law at first reading. A resident at a May 21, 2019 hearing (initials not certain from the diarized transcript) had cited the fire commissioner as saying many places in Steinbach were not safe to live in.
notes: Unanimous at first reading; no divided vote. The May 12, 2020 SPC report and the agenda package (page 35) were not in our files. The Sept 15, 2020 video failed to download; its minutes mention nothing on By-law 2157.

title: First St rezoning approved; derelict houses to be replaced by apartments
summary: At the hearing on By-law 2148 (78 First St, 10 units), a nearby resident welcomed the removal of derelict houses on First Street but worried about the pace of development. Councillor Siemens said the area's derelict housing showed it was under revitalization, as the community plan intended. Council gave second and third readings unanimously.
status_detail: Second and third readings carried unanimously (R20-127, R20-128), subject to a development agreement.
reasons: already-doing-enough: Older areas with derelict housing are being revitalized through redevelopment under the community plan. (Jac Siemens)
public: I. (Westdale St; first name only given) said derelict houses on First Street needed to be dealt with and welcomed it, but questioned the pace of development.
notes: Similar 2018 comments: a May 1, 2018 applicant described 'a bunch of old rundown houses' on First Street to be replaced.

title: Dwelling Safety Standards By-law 2157 adopted: alarms and safe exits in every home, aimed at secondary suites
themes: secondary-suites; rental; landlords; property-standards; fines; enforcement
summary: Council gave second and third reading to By-law 2157 on Jan 5, 2021 (first reading Sept 1, 2020). It sets minimum life-safety standards for every dwelling unit: smoke alarms, carbon monoxide alarms and a safe exit, with secondary (basement) suites the main target. Staff said compliance was expected to be mostly voluntary, with inspections when owners or tenants ask; council members said the rules were basic and not onerous.
status_detail: Adopted unanimously. A public awareness campaign followed in 2021. By Aug 2024 staff reported only 'several dozen' of possibly several hundred suites had come forward, and announced proactive enforcement (see 2024-secondary-suite-enforcement).
figures: Approx. cost to bring a suite up to standard 'plus or minus $3,000' and about 500 city staff hours in the first year (Councillor Siemens citing the agenda notes, transcript 0:25:16); about a dozen public comments, mostly in favour, and several hundred views of the information video (City Manager, 0:26:48). Fine $1,000, each day a separate offence (by-law text per existing report; not re-checked here).
reasons: complaint-driven: Inspection rules for dwellings are strict, so the city expected mostly voluntary compliance and inspections on request from owners or tenants, though it kept a list of properties it would like to inspect. (Troy Warkentin); affordability: Noted the work could cost about $3,000 per suite and 500 staff hours in year one, while saying it protects marginalized residents. (Jac Siemens)
public: No delegations. Staff reported about a dozen online comments, mostly supportive.
notes: No speaker map for 2021; speakers identified from chair's addresses and minutes. Fine amount not mentioned in the 2021 transcript.

title: Community services/safety officer appointed weed inspector every year
summary: Each spring council appointed the city's community services officer (from 2026, two community safety officers) as municipal weed inspector under the provincial Noxious Weeds Act. Members treated it as housekeeping.
status_detail: Appointed every year 2021-2026: Trevor Schellenberg (2021-2023), Grant Ryland (2024-2025), Grant Ryland and Kevin Williams (2026). No report on weed complaints or orders came to council.
mover: B. Hiebert (2021); Zwaagstra (2022, 2023); S. Penner (2024, 2026); D. Penner (2025)
seconder: Zwaagstra (2021); B. Hiebert (2022, 2026); J. Hiebert (2023); Siemens (2024); Zwaagstra (2025)
notes: Mover/seconder per motions CSV; the 2026 resolution number appears to be a typo in the minutes.

title: By-law enforcement staffing: one community services officer, two by 2026
summary: Financial plan presentations in 2021 and 2025 listed a single community services officer 'to enforce city bylaws'. In 2023 council set up a self-funded Community Safety Officer program (for vehicle weight limits). By March 2026 two community safety officers were appointed weed inspectors, and in July 2026 staff proposed buying a second CSO truck with a provincial safety grant; council deferred the grant to committee.
status_detail: A second officer was added by 2026. The grant allocation (including the $65,000 truck) was deferred to a committee meeting; no public decision found by Nov 2026. Council received no enforcement statistics (complaints, notices, cleanups) in this period.
figures: 2021 plan: 16 RCMP, 44 firefighters, 8 fire trucks, one community services officer (transcript 2021-04-06 0:19:59). 2025 plan: 47 firefighters, 8 trucks, one community services officer (2025-03-04 0:06:04). 2026 grant: $200,000; $65,000 proposed for a second CSO truck, $135,000 for cameras (minutes Jul 21, 2026). CSO program for weight restrictions R23-036 (Feb 21, 2023, Zwaagstra/Siemens, unanimous).
notes: 2023-02-21 has no transcript; R23-036 from minutes. CSOs' encampment work is covered in the homelessness topic.

title: Administrative Penalty By-law 2173: more by-laws brought under ticket-style penalty notices
summary: By-law 2173 amended Schedule A of the Administrative Penalty By-law 2076 so that more city by-laws can be enforced with penalty notices under the provincial Municipal By-law Enforcement Act. Staff said it gives 'additional tools to our bylaw and animal control'; Councillor Zwaagstra said it lets fines be adjudicated more quickly.
status_detail: First reading May 4, second and third June 1, 2021, all unanimous. Which by-laws were added was not stated in the meeting; the existing report notes the Dwelling Safety Standards by-law is on the penalty schedule ($1,000, $500 early payment) while the Junk, Weeds & Nuisance By-law 1663 is not.
figures: Discussed at the April 13, 2021 Strategic Priorities Committee (Adam Thiessen, 0:28:33). Schedule contents not checked (no package on file).
seconder: Jac Siemens (1st); Jake Hiebert (2nd); Bill Hiebert (3rd)
notes: Exact list of by-laws added to Schedule A in 2021 not verified.

title: Neighbours raise run-down rentals, long grass and garbage at development hearings
themes: residents; rental; landlords; unsightly; weeds; garbage; derelict
summary: At hearings from 2021 to 2026 neighbours judged proposals by how existing rentals on or near the site were kept: rentals with police visits (Hanover St 2021, Third St 2023), low upkeep and blowing garbage (First St and Home St 2024), 18-inch grass and weeds (Henry St 2025), garbage spilling onto a church yard (McKenzie Ave 2026) and renters who 'aren't going to look after it' (Giesbrecht St 2026). Council decided each file on land-use grounds; none led to a property-standards response.
status_detail: Outcomes: Hanover St variance approved 2021 (R21-189); Third St rezoning denied 2023 (R23-160, unanimous, on density/consultation grounds); Home St second reading 4-3 2024 (R24-061); First St variance approved 2024 (R24-063); Henry St variance and rezoning approved 2025 (R25-093, R25-094/095); McKenzie Ave approved 2026 (R26-068); Giesbrecht St second reading 2026 (R26-179). No enforcement review or report followed.
reasons: private-property: Upkeep was treated as outside the land-use question; members cited density, fit and consultation instead. (council (implicit))
public: Residents (M.R., L.A., G.F., E.D., R.B., E.B., C.M., H.K., T.N.) described poorly kept rentals, police visits, long grass and garbage; all claims are unproven and no owner is identified here. Some applicants and owners agreed properties were run down and said redevelopment would fix them.
vote: unanimous except R24-061 4-3 (against: D. Penner, J. Hiebert, Zwaagstra)
notes: Residents identified by initials; property owners not named. Hearing outcomes from minutes; the split vote R24-061 is a rezoning decided on density/fit, not on property standards.

title: Unpaid city invoices transferred to property taxes several times a year
summary: Council regularly added unpaid accounts receivable to owners' tax rolls, described by the mayor as housekeeping. These can include cleanup charges under By-law 1663, but the resolutions do not say what the invoices were for.
status_detail: Carried unanimously each time; purpose of the charges not disclosed.
notes: Cannot verify whether any of these were property-standards cleanups.

title: Housing charity describes a cold, unsafe basement suite while seeking approval for affordable units
summary: Presenting its 24-unit affordable building (parking variance), Steinbach Community Outreach's executive director described a former client raising her daughter in a basement suite heated only by plug-in heaters and an open oven door, and said all new units would be above ground. Council approved the variance.
status_detail: The variance was approved (R22-052, unanimous). Heating and other living conditions inside rentals were not discussed further; By-law 2157 covers alarms and exits, not heat.
figures: 24 units, bachelor and 1-bedroom; 30 parking stalls instead of 40 (City Manager).
public: I.K. (Steinbach Community Outreach) described substandard basement-suite living; claims are the speaker's own.

title: Resident reports overflowing apartment dumpsters and litter near Woodhaven Ave
summary: At the hearing on the Woodhaven Ave affordable-housing variance, a Whitby Cres resident said the existing apartments' dumpsters were 'typically really full' and overflowing, alongside litter, theft and people cutting through yards. The mayor said littering and theft were matters for the RCMP and that the new building's dumpster would be fenced.
status_detail: Variance approved unanimously; a dumpster enclosure was expected for the new building. No action on the overflowing bins at the existing buildings was recorded.
reasons: enforcement-limits: Littering and theft are for the RCMP. (Earl Funk)
public: N.P. (Whitby Cres) described overflowing dumpsters and litter at nearby apartments; unproven.

title: Penalty schedule amended (By-law 2209) for burning, business licence and pool by-laws
summary: A housekeeping amendment to the administrative penalty schedule so fines under the new burning, business licence and swimming pool by-laws could be enforced. Junk, weeds and nuisance (By-law 1663) were not part of it.
status_detail: Three readings carried unanimously.
seconder: D. Penner (1st); S. Penner (2nd); D. Penner (3rd)

title: Council looks to redevelopment and demolitions to replace neglected and derelict rentals
summary: Several members and applicants described infill and demolition as the answer to neglected housing: Councillor D. Penner said infill usually comes to areas 'neglected for years', Councillor Siemens welcomed demolition permits because 'derelict homes' would come out, and the mayor said a new building's dumpster would end loose garbage at a Henry St rental. No vacant or derelict building by-law was proposed.
status_detail: Individual run-down rentals were replaced through redevelopment (e.g. Henry St, First St). No by-law on derelict or vacant buildings, and no enforcement against them, was discussed.
figures: Dec 2024: three demolition permits (two First St, one Walnut) (Councillor Siemens 0:49:09).
reasons: already-doing-enough: Redevelopment is expected to clear neglected properties. (Damian Penner; Jac Siemens; Earl Funk)
public: Applicant L.W. said older infill homes 'becoming derelict' are too costly to renovate (Nov 2022). Applicant J.L. (May 2025) agreed the Henry St house had 'fallen into a state of neglect'.

title: Voluntary compliance with By-law 2157 judged insufficient; proactive suite enforcement and $1,000/day fines backed
summary: On Aug 20, 2024 the City Manager reported that of possibly several hundred secondary suites only several dozen had come forward since 2021, and that several recent house fires involved non-compliant basement suites. The city would contact owners believed to have suites, place work orders on title if needed, possibly decommission suites, and run a media campaign. Every member spoke in support, including fines of up to $1,000 a day; Councillor Siemens warned low-rent units could be lost.
status_detail: No resolution (an update; minutes record members 'voiced their support'). No report on suites contacted, inspected, ordered, decommissioned or fined came back to council through Nov 3, 2026.
figures: 'up to several hundred' suites, 'several dozen' compliant (City Manager 0:13:28); maximum fine $1,000 per day (0:17:25).
reasons: affordability: Council held off on enforcement because it could cost many low-end rental units at a time of homelessness. (Jac Siemens); complaint-driven: Voluntary compliance remains 'much preferred'; fines are a last resort. (Troy Warkentin); cost: Holding all suites to the National Building Code would have meant significant decommissioning, so council chose basic life-safety standards instead. (Troy Warkentin)
notes: Jake Hiebert's label is medium in the speaker map; raised to high on the chair's address immediately before the turn.

title: Administrative Penalty By-law 2259 adds traffic and animal control fines; junk and weeds still not ticketable
summary: First reading Dec 17, 2024 and second and third Jan 21, 2025. The by-law replaced Schedule A of Administrative Penalty By-law 2076 so the new traffic and animal control fines could be issued by by-law enforcement staff. Staff said the rest of the schedule stayed as it was; the Junk, Weeds & Nuisance By-law 1663 was not added.
status_detail: Adopted unanimously. No property-standards fines were added.
notes: Contents of Schedule A taken from the existing report (Dec 17, 2024 package).

title: Limiting vehicles per rental unit: city says it does not enforce on private property
summary: At a Nov 2025 hearing on a multi-unit rental near PTH 52, Councillor Siemens asked whether a development agreement could limit vehicles per unit. The City Manager said zoning only sets parking stalls, and limiting vehicles would mean enforcement 'not something the city does on private property'; the applicant said the landlord could limit occupants and vehicles through leases.
status_detail: No condition on vehicles or occupancy was imposed; the variance passed 5-2 (R25-222) on other grounds.
reasons: private-property: The city does not enforce rules inside private property; the landlord must police it. (Troy Warkentin)
public: Applicant T.T. said lease terms could limit occupants and vehicles.
notes: The 5-2 vote was on the variance (parking/size), not on property standards.

title: New Zoning By-law 2245 requires screened garbage areas; staff flag an inadequate bin area
summary: The new zoning by-law (third reading Jan 20, 2026) requires landscaping plans with screened refuse containment for anything larger than a duplex and requires landscaped areas to be kept free of refuse. In March 2026 the City Manager relayed the city engineer's view that a seniors' building plan's garbage area was inadequate; in October the mayor told a neighbour the city has 'strict regulations' on bins.
status_detail: Adopted (R26-015, unanimous). Site-plan review checks bin areas; no rule on how often apartment bins are emptied. The March 2026 hearing was adjourned to April (R26-059, 6-1, Siemens against).
public: E.H. (Kootenay Way, Oct 2026) asked that an apartment's two bins be moved away from his house; the developer said the city requires a concrete enclosure.
notes: Zoning By-law 2245 refuse provisions per the existing report (s. 7.5 and landscaping plan rules); R26-059 vote from motions CSV.

title: Penalty schedule updated for the new Land Drainage By-law; 'educate, then enforce, then penalize'
summary: By-law 2282 amended the administrative penalty schedule to carry fines for the new Land Drainage By-law 2274 (sump pumps, nuisance water). Councillor D. Penner said the city's approach is to educate first, then enforce, then penalize.
status_detail: Adopted unanimously. Not presented as adding the junk and weeds by-law.
reasons: complaint-driven: Penalties are a backstop: educate, enforce, then penalize; inspectors are not out looking to fine people. (Damian Penner)
notes: Text of By-law 2282 not reviewed.
